title: JavaScript → TypeScript → React
description: Start with browser and JavaScript fundamentals, then build a typed, accessible learning tracker with React.
prerequisites: No React experience required. Be comfortable creating folders and editing text files.
Work through JavaScript lessons before the React sections. Familiarity with HTML is useful but introduced here.
outcomes: Model information with JavaScript arrays and objects.
Use TypeScript to describe values and handle optional data.
Build components, forms and state transitions without mutating previous state.
Explain loading, error and empty states, then test a small tracker.
setup: JavaScript console examples run in a browser developer console or Node.js. Never paste untrusted code into a signed-in website’s console.
For React lessons, create a separate practice project using the official React build-from-scratch guide and a current supported Node.js version that meets your chosen tool’s requirements.

A learning-only Vite setup: npm create vite@latest notebook-practice -- --template react-ts; cd notebook-practice; npm install; npm run dev. These commands download tools; this notebook does not run them.

Replace src/App.tsx with the downloadable example for the capstone. Keep the generated main.tsx. Remove starter App.css imports if experimenting with appearance. Run npm run build to type-check/build.
nextSteps: Add routing with a maintained router and study URL/history behavior.
Add server persistence, authentication and API validation; browser storage is not an access-control boundary.
Learn a framework’s data loading, server rendering and deployment before building production applications.
Practise automated component tests, browser tests, performance profiling and accessibility audits.

lessons.title: 1. The browser, HTML and JavaScript
lessons.takeaway: HTML gives meaning, CSS controls presentation and JavaScript changes behavior.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: A browser turns a document into an interactive page. A button has a role, focus behavior and keyboard activation that a clickable div does not automatically provide. Start with meaningful elements before styling.

The tiny example is a complete HTML fragment. Its label tells a user what the input means. A React application still produces ordinary browser elements; React is not a replacement for HTML or accessibility.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: A placeholder disappears when typing and is not a substitute for a persistent label. Avoid using color alone to indicate errors.

exercise.prompt: Write markup for a study-minutes number input with a label and a Save button.
exercise.solution:
<label for="minutes">Study minutes</label>
<input id="minutes" type="number" min="0" />
<button type="button">Save</button>
checks: Clicking the label focuses the input.
Tab reaches the input and button.
This markup does not save anything until behavior is added.

quiz.question: Which element already supports keyboard activation?
options: A span with a click handler
quiz.explanation: Native controls provide useful behavior and semantics. Styling a generic element does not add them.

lessons.title: 2. Values, equality and conversion
lessons.takeaway: Convert at boundaries; do not rely on accidental coercion.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: Input values arrive as strings even when they look numeric. Convert deliberately, then validate. Number('') is zero, so check for blank input before conversion.

const prevents reassignment of the binding; it does not freeze an object. Use strict equality to compare values without automatic type conversion. A missing value may be undefined; intentional absence often uses null.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: Treating every falsy value as missing rejects valid zero. Check the condition you actually mean.

exercise.prompt: Write parseMinutes(raw) that returns null for blanks, negatives or non-integers.
checks: Zero is accepted.
Blank and fractional input are rejected.
Use null explicitly rather than testing result with !result.

quiz.question: What is Number('')?
quiz.explanation: An empty string converts to zero; validate blank input before converting.

lessons.title: 3. Arrays, objects and transformations
lessons.takeaway: Keep source records separate from derived views.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: An array is an ordered collection. An object groups named properties for one record. map transforms every element, filter selects elements and reduce combines them into one value.
A learning tracker can store records once and derive completed titles or totals when needed. A derived array need not be another mutable source of truth.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: sort mutates an array. Use [...items].sort(...) when the original order must remain intact. A shallow copy still shares nested objects.

exercise.prompt: Return total minutes for completed records only.
checks: The result is 35.
An empty array returns 0.
The input records remain unchanged.

quiz.question: Which operation selects a subset?
quiz.explanation: filter keeps matching elements. map transforms elements without changing the count.

lessons.title: 4. Functions and predictable behavior
lessons.takeaway: A small pure function is easier to explain and test.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: A function receives inputs and returns an output. A pure function depends only on its inputs and does not change external state. Logging and network calls are side effects; they are useful, but keep them at clear boundaries.
Arrow functions are concise syntax, not a separate execution model. A function passed as an argument can be called later; calling it immediately passes its result instead.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: Returning nothing yields undefined. In an arrow function with braces, write return explicitly.

exercise.prompt: Implement toggleById(rows, id) without changing rows or its objects.
checks: The selected item flips.
An unknown ID leaves all values unchanged.
The original selected object is not mutated.

quiz.question: What should an event handler receive?
options: Always the result of calling a function now
quiz.explanation: Passing a function defers work until the event occurs.

lessons.title: 5. Promises and API boundaries
lessons.takeaway: An asynchronous result needs success, failure and loading behavior.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: A Promise represents eventual completion or failure. await pauses the current async function, not the whole browser. Use try/catch to handle rejections and decide what the user should see.
fetch resolves for many HTTP errors, including 404; inspect response.ok. JSON parsing is not schema validation. Treat external data as untrusted and check its shape before using it.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: Launching dependent requests simultaneously can use data that is not ready. Conversely, unrelated requests can often run together with Promise.all; one rejection rejects that combined promise.

exercise.prompt: Handle a simulated rejection and return an empty list only after explicitly recording the error.
checks: The rejection is handled.
The fallback is deliberate, not a silent success.
In a UI, display an error and retry option rather than disguising failure as an empty dataset.

quiz.question: Does fetch automatically reject on HTTP 404?
quiz.explanation: Check response.ok or status; an HTTP response can resolve the promise even when its status is an error.

lessons.title: 6. TypeScript and narrowing
lessons.takeaway: Types check assumptions during development; validate external data at runtime.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: TypeScript adds a static type checker to JavaScript. A union such as string | null describes alternatives. A conditional can narrow that union before an operation is used.
An interface describes an expected shape, but it does not inspect a network response. Casting with as does not make unknown data valid. Start with unknown at external boundaries and check it.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: any disables useful checking. Prefer a specific type or unknown with narrowing when the shape is not yet established.

exercise.prompt: Accept unknown and return a nonnegative integer or null.
checks: String '3' is not accepted as a number.
Negative, fractional and NaN values return null.
No unsafe assertion is needed.

quiz.question: Does an interface validate JSON?
quiz.explanation: Types are not runtime validators; a server can return data that violates your declared type.

lessons.title: 7. Components, props and lists
lessons.takeaway: Pass data down and keep each component’s responsibility clear.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: A component renders one part of the interface from its inputs. Props are supplied by its parent. Begin with a static screen so the component boundaries are understandable before adding behavior.

Use stable record IDs for list keys. The key helps React match elements between renders; it is not an ordinary prop automatically received by the child. In the snippet, the parent passes title separately.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: Array indexes are fragile keys when records can be inserted, deleted or reordered. Do not generate new random keys on every render.

exercise.prompt: Extend LessonRow to display a completed marker using a done prop.
checks: Complete and To do are visible text.
Props are not modified by the component.
The parent supplies the status.

quiz.question: Which key is most appropriate for reorderable records?
options: A new random number every render
quiz.explanation: A stable identity lets React match the same record through list changes.

lessons.title: 8. Events, state and immutable updates
lessons.takeaway: State is a snapshot; request the next state instead of mutating the current one.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: React state retains information between renders. A setter requests another render. The current event handler still sees the snapshot from the render that created it.

When an update depends on previous state, a functional updater communicates that dependency. Create new arrays and changed objects so the update is explicit. Keep calculated totals derived from the current records.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: Directly changing an object in state does not request a render. Also avoid storing both records and a separately maintained completed count when the count can be derived.

exercise.prompt: Write the state update to toggle record id 'types'.
checks: The selected object is copied.
Unchanged records retain their values.
A second toggle returns to the original status.

quiz.question: What does a state setter do?
options: Mutates the current local variable immediately
Requests a future render with updated state
quiz.explanation: The current render’s snapshot remains unchanged; a new render receives the next state.

frames.label: Render one
frames.explanation: The handler closes over this render’s snapshot.

frames.label: User clicks
frames.explanation: The updater computes the next count. The current snapshot is still zero.

frames.label: Render two
frames.explanation: React renders using the next state and updates the visible result.

lessons.title: 9. Forms, validation and derived views
lessons.takeaway: Store user input; derive filtered output from it.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: A controlled input receives its value from state and reports changes through an event handler. Keep the input’s accessible label visible. A form can handle submission from both a button and the Enter key.
Search results are derived from records plus the search query. There is no need to copy them into another state variable. Validate on submit, and explain errors in text near the field.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: This is a component fragment, not a full file. Hooks must be called at the top level of a component or custom Hook, not inside a conditional.

exercise.prompt: Describe and implement a trimmed title validator.
checks: Whitespace-only input fails.
A valid title is trimmed.
Show a visible error; do not rely on an alert or red border alone.

quiz.question: Should filtered results usually be stored separately?
options: No, calculate them from records and query
quiz.explanation: A derived value avoids synchronizing duplicate state.

lessons.title: 10. Effects and external systems
lessons.takeaway: Use Effects to synchronize external systems, not to calculate ordinary derived values.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: An Effect can connect a component to something outside rendering, such as browser storage or a subscription. Cleanup releases resources or prevents obsolete work from affecting the current screen.

Fetching data in an Effect needs loading and error handling plus protection from stale results. Frameworks and data libraries can manage these concerns. Do not suppress dependencies just to stop an Effect from running.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: An Effect may be set up and cleaned up extra times in development Strict Mode. Design correct cleanup instead of relying on a single execution.

exercise.prompt: Choose whether a completed count needs an Effect, then implement it.
exercise.solution:
const completedCount = lessons.filter(row => row.done).length;
// Derived during rendering; no Effect or separate count state required.
checks: Changing lessons changes the count on the next render.
No extra synchronization step exists.
Use Effects only for actual external synchronization.

quiz.question: Which operation needs no Effect?
options: Subscribing to an external event source
quiz.explanation: Pure calculations can run during rendering.

lessons.title: 11. Build and test a learning tracker
lessons.takeaway: Finish a small complete feature before adding a larger architecture.

sections.title: Build the mental model
paragraphs: Download App.tsx and run it in the React TypeScript project from setup. It has a search input, stable IDs, toggles and a derived completion count. It deliberately keeps data in memory so state behavior is visible without storage complications.

Test behavior through the screen: keyboard focus, blank search, mixed-case search, toggling, and an empty result. Then change one requirement at a time. Treat loading, failure and server validation as separate work when adding an API.
sections.example:
Acceptance scenario:
1. Initial count: 0 of 3 complete.
2. Mark Types complete: 1 of 3 complete.
3. Search STATE: one record remains visible.
4. Clear search: Types remains complete.
5. Refresh: in-memory state resets.

sections.title: Common mistake to avoid
paragraphs: Do not claim persistence just because a value survives changing a filter. This example resets after a page reload and has no backend.

exercise.prompt: Add a Show incomplete only checkbox and combine it with text filtering.
checks: Both filters apply together.
The total completion count still reflects all records.
An empty list has an explanatory message.

quiz.question: What must be added for progress across devices?
options: A persistence/synchronization design, usually involving a backend
quiz.explanation: Memory state is local to a running page. Cross-device data needs storage, identity and synchronization decisions.
